newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria seeks to clear up Pope attack rumours.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria seeks to clear up Pope attack rumours.

text.p: Bulgaria said on Wednesday it wanted Germany to help put an end to fresh speculation about a "Bulgarian connection" in a 1981 attempt on the life of Pope John Paul.
The German mass-circulation daily Bild said last month that former communist East German intelligence files implied Bulgaria's communist-era secret service had been involved in the attack.

"Following a series of articles published in the German media...Bulgaria has sent a letter to the German authorities demanding to clear up the matter," Foreign Ministry spokesman Radko Vlaikov told a news conference.

"In the letter Foreign Minister Nadezhda Mihailova and Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev are pressing the German authorities to cooperate and present the documents cited by the media if they really exist," said Vlaikov.
He said the matter affected not just politicians, but the Bulgarian nation as a whole. "The whole truth must come to light," he said.

Bild said on June 17 that an Italian magistrate had visited Berlin in April to seek help with his inquiry into the attack, and had met a former officer from East Berlin's Ministry for State Security (Stasi).

According to Bild, the ex-officer said the Bulgarian secret service had asked the Stasi to help deflect suspicion that Sofia was behind the shooting in St Peter's Square in Rome, which seriously injured the Pope.
"There is no doubt that discovering the whole truth will clear the stains from Bulgaria's reputation," Vlaikov said.

"At the same time, if there is evidence for Bulgaria's involvement in the assassination attempt, it should be presented (to Bulgaria) and those who incited it should bear their responsibility and be charged," he said.

Mehmet Ali Agca, the Turk who shot the Pope on May 13, 1981 and is now serving a life sentence in Italy, has said the Soviet KGB and the Bulgarian government of communist leader Todor Zhivkov were behind the attack.

At his trial Agca claimed the KGB had enlisted the Bulgarian secret service to kill the Pope because of his support for the Solidarity union in his Polish homeland, which was threatening Moscow's grip on eastern Europe.
Later Agca said he had acted alone.

Three Turks and three Bulgarians charged with conspiring with Agca were acquitted for lack of evidence -- an Italian formula meaning the court was not fully convinced of their innocence but could not prove their guilt.
Since then the Bulgarian connection has neither been proved nor completely quashed.

In April this year Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov, elected on the ticket of the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces, invited Pope John Paul to make a first visit to the predominantly Orthodox Balkan state.
